comments.author: BoppreH
comments.text:
If you're on Python and your problem is too big for a single regex, but too small for a full-blown parser like in the article, I can recommend the built-in re.Scanner[0]. It's a regex-based tokenizer[1] (so no recursive parsing) in the `re` module, that for reasons is completely missing from any official documentation.
You give it a pattern for each token type, and a function to process each match, and you get back a list of processed tokens.
Importantly, it processes the list in one pass and ensures the matches are contiguous, where a naive `re.findall` with capture groups will ignore unmatched characters. You also get a reference to the running scanner, so you can record the location of the match for reporting errors.
import re
# Initialize the scanner.
scanner = re.Scanner([
(r"\d+",   lambda scanner, token: ('COUNT', int(token))),
(r"\w+",   lambda scanner, token: ('ANIMAL', token.removesuffix('s'))),
(r"[,. ]",     None), # None -> skip token.
])
# Scan a sample string.
results, remainder = scanner.scan("45 pigeons, 23 cows, 11 spiders.")
# Ensure we parsed the whole thing.
assert not remainder
print(results)
# [('COUNT', 45),
#  ('ANIMAL', 'pigeon'),
#  ('COUNT', 23),
#  ('AN

comments.author: ArneCode
comments.text:
I really like the animations, makes it intuitive to understand what is happening!
One disadvantage that I think parser combinators have, for example compared to parser generator libraries (where the parser is generated from a seperate grammar file), is that you have to add a lot of mapping / unwrapping code. In my opinion this makes the parsers harder to read.
As an attempt to improve this, I have been working on a parser combinator library in rust.
It adds two extra combinators (capture and bind) which can store the results of parsers in buckets (bind) and use the values stored in these buckets later to construct results (capture).
This allows you to eliminate the unwrapping / mapping code and seperate the grammar from the result contstruction.
If you have the time, I would really appreciate feedback on this!
You can find it here:
https://github.com/ArneCode/marser

comments.author: skew-aberration
comments.text:
Coral gets its color from algae called zooxanthellae, which it depends on for photosynthesis.
Bleaching is actually due to the coral expelling those algae. Bleached corals are not dead, and remarkably they can not only let the algae in again but can also select a different algae species to cultivate (changing colour in the process)!.
This is thought to be a deliberate survival strategy to optimize the species of algae under different conditions (Adaptive Bleaching Hypothesis).
Bleaching is caused by the same stressors (like high temperature) which kill coral, but bleaching itself is not death of the coral.
